questions.prompt: Which data structure does breadth-first search use to order its exploration?
questions.explanation: BFS dequeues a vertex and enqueues its unvisited neighbours, so nodes are visited in order of increasing distance from the source. The FIFO queue is what produces the level-by-level order.

questions.prompt: On an unweighted graph, breadth-first search from a source finds:

options.text: The longest path to every vertex
The shortest path in edges to every reachable vertex

questions.explanation: Because BFS expands vertices in distance order, the first time it reaches a vertex is via a shortest path. This guarantee holds only when all edges have equal weight.

questions.prompt: Depth-first search is naturally implemented using:
questions.explanation: DFS goes as deep as possible before backtracking, which the call stack (or an explicit stack) captures directly. Swapping the stack for a queue turns DFS into BFS.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of BFS or DFS on a graph with V vertices and E edges using an adjacency list?
questions.explanation: Each vertex is processed once and each edge examined once across all adjacency lists, giving O(V + E). On an adjacency matrix the traversal is O(V^2).

questions.prompt: How can DFS detect a cycle in a directed graph?

options.text: By checking the number of connected components
By counting the number of edges
By finding a back edge to a vertex currently on the recursion stack

questions.explanation: A vertex still in the active recursion (grey) that is reached again indicates a back edge, which closes a cycle. Tracking three colours (white, grey, black) distinguishes back edges from forward and cross edges.

questions.prompt: To count the connected components of an undirected graph, you can:

options.text: Count the edges and divide by two
Run a single BFS from vertex 0
Run a traversal from each unvisited vertex and count how many traversals you start

questions.explanation: Each fresh traversal marks one entire component; the number of fresh starts is the component count. A single traversal only reaches the component containing its start vertex.

questions.prompt: Which traversal is better suited to finding the shortest path in an unweighted maze?

options.text: BFS, because it explores in order of distance
DFS, because it goes deep first

questions.explanation: BFS reaches every cell by a fewest-moves path, so the first time it hits the target is optimal. DFS may reach the target by a long, winding route first.

questions.prompt: In a DFS of a directed acyclic graph, listing vertices in decreasing order of their finish times yields:
questions.explanation: A vertex finishes only after all vertices reachable from it, so ordering by decreasing finish time places every vertex before its descendants. This is the DFS-based topological sort.

questions.prompt: What is the space complexity of BFS in the worst case?

options.text: O(V), for the queue and visited set

questions.explanation: In the worst case the queue holds a whole level of vertices, which can be O(V), and the visited set is also O(V). DFS uses O(V) for its stack in the worst case too.

questions.prompt: How can BFS be used to test whether an undirected graph is bipartite?

options.text: Check whether it has a cycle of any length
Two-colour vertices level by level; a conflict between adjacent same-colour vertices means it is not bipartite
Count the total number of edges

questions.explanation: Assigning alternating colours across BFS levels works exactly when the graph has no odd cycle. Finding an edge joining two vertices of the same colour reveals such an odd cycle.
